title: 🎯 Why Measurement Errors Are JEE Gold

sections.heading: The Real-World Problem
sections.body:
Every measurement in physics carries an **error** — no instrument is perfect.

JEE Main tests 3 key skills from this topic:
• Calculate the **least count** of an instrument
• Find **errors** in derived quantities
• Express answers with correct **significant figures**

sections.heading: How Many Marks?
sections.body:
2–3 questions per JEE Main paper come directly from this chapter.

Mastering error propagation alone can secure **10+ marks** in a year — virtually free marks once you know the rules.

highlight: Least count + error propagation + significant figures = 3 pillars of this chapter.

title: Accuracy vs Precision — The Target Analogy
caption: Accuracy = closeness to the true value. Precision = closeness of measurements to each other.

title: Types of Errors in Measurement

sections.heading: 1. Systematic Errors
sections.body:
Consistent errors that occur in the **same direction** every time.
• **Instrumental error**: zero error in Vernier/screw gauge
• **Personal error**: parallax, reaction time
• **Environmental error**: temperature, humidity effects

→ These reduce **accuracy** (shift the mean from true value).

sections.heading: 2. Random Errors
sections.body:
Unpredictable, fluctuating errors in **both directions**.
• Cause: unpredictable environmental fluctuations
• **Fix**: take more readings and average them

→ These reduce **precision** but average out over many readings.

sections.heading: 3. Gross Errors
sections.body:
Human blunders — misreading scale, wrong units, calculation errors.

**Fix**: Repeat carefully. These cannot be analysed statistically.

highlight: Random errors → reduced by averaging. Systematic errors → identified and corrected. Gross errors → avoided by care.

title: Vernier Caliper — How It Works
caption: The Vernier scale slides along the main scale. The coinciding division gives extra precision.

title: Vernier Caliper — Deep Dive

sections.heading: The Key Principle
sections.body:
n VSD = (n−1) MSD

This tiny mismatch between scales is the entire secret of the Vernier caliper.

For standard: **10 VSD = 9 MSD** → 1 VSD = 0.9 mm → LC = 0.1 mm

sections.heading: Reading Formula
sections.body:
**Total Reading = MS reading + (Coinciding VSD × LC)**

• MS reading: last main scale division *before* the Vernier zero
• Coinciding VSD: Vernier division that aligns exactly with any MS line

sections.heading: Zero Error
sections.body:
• **Positive zero error**: Vernier 0 is right of MS 0 → subtract from reading
• **Negative zero error**: Vernier 0 is left of MS 0 → add to reading

**Corrected reading = Raw reading − Zero error**

highlight: Golden rule: ALWAYS correct for zero error BEFORE reporting the final measurement.

title: Vernier Caliper — Least Count

parts.meaning: Total number of Vernier scale divisions

note: Standard Vernier: n=10, MSD=1mm → LC = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm
derived_from: n VSD = (n−1) MSD → 1 VSD = (n−1)/n MSD → LC = 1 − (n−1)/n = 1/n MSD

title: Tap to Reveal: Steps to Read a Vernier Caliper
instruction: Tap each step to see the procedure.

items.back: Close the jaws without any object. Note if Vernier 0 coincides with MS 0. Record the zero error.
Place the object. Read the last main scale division BEFORE the Vernier zero mark.
Find the Vernier division that coincides EXACTLY with any main scale line. That number is the Vernier reading.
Total Reading = MS reading + (Vernier reading × LC)

Corrected Reading = Total Reading − Zero Error

Positive zero error → subtract it. Negative zero error → add it.

question: A Vernier caliper has 10 VSD = 9 MSD. If 1 MSD = 1 mm, the least count is:
explanation:
LC = 1/n × MSD = 1/10 × 1 mm = **0.1 mm** ✓

Alternatively:
1 VSD = 9/10 mm = 0.9 mm
LC = 1.0 − 0.9 = 0.1 mm
hint: LC = 1 MSD / n, where n is the number of Vernier divisions.

title: Screw Gauge — Schematic Diagram
caption: Each full rotation of the thimble moves it by exactly 1 pitch along the barrel.

title: Screw Gauge — How It Works

sections.heading: Key Components
sections.body:
• **Barrel**: Fixed, shows the main scale (0.5 mm or 1 mm divisions)
• **Thimble**: Rotates, has N circular scale divisions (CSD)
• **Pitch**: Linear distance moved per complete rotation

sections.heading: Least Count
sections.body:
**LC = Pitch / N**

Common combinations:
• Pitch = 1 mm, N = 100 → LC = **0.01 mm**
• Pitch = 0.5 mm, N = 50 → LC = **0.01 mm**

Both give the same 0.01 mm = 10 µm!

sections.heading: Zero Error & Backlash
sections.body:
• **Positive zero error**: thimble reads positive when jaws just touch → subtract
• **Negative zero error**: thimble reads negative → add
• **Backlash error**: play in screw → always rotate thimble in one direction only

highlight: Screw gauge (0.01 mm) is 10× finer than Vernier caliper (0.1 mm). It measures wire diameters and thin sheets.

title: Screw Gauge — Least Count

parts.meaning: Linear distance moved per complete rotation (mm)
Number of divisions on the circular scale

note: Reading = Main scale reading + (CSD coinciding × LC) − Zero error
derived_from: In one full rotation, thimble moves exactly 1 pitch. Each of the N divisions = Pitch/N of linear distance.

question: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on the circular scale. What is its least count?
explanation:
LC = Pitch / N = 0.5 mm / 50 = **0.01 mm** ✓

Key insight: Halving both pitch and N gives the same LC.
Screw gauge always achieves 0.01 mm with standard combinations.
hint: LC = Pitch ÷ (Number of circular scale divisions)

sentence: A Vernier caliper with 20 VSD equal to 19 MSD (1 MSD = 1 mm) has a least count of _______.
explanation:
LC = 1/n × MSD = 1/20 × 1 mm = **0.05 mm** ✓

Verification: 1 VSD = 19/20 mm = 0.95 mm → LC = 1 − 0.95 = 0.05 mm

instruction: Match each instrument to its typical least count:
explanation:
Metre scale: least count = smallest graduation = 1 mm.
Vernier (10): LC = 1/10 mm = 0.1 mm.
Vernier (20): LC = 1/20 mm = 0.05 mm.
Screw gauge: LC = 1/100 mm = 0.01 mm (10× finer than Vernier).

title: Absolute Error & True Value

sections.heading: What is the True Value?
sections.body:
We can never know the exact true value.

Instead, we take the **arithmetic mean** of n repeated measurements as our best estimate:

**ā = (a₁ + a₂ + ... + aₙ) / n**

sections.heading: Absolute Error
sections.body:
For each measurement aᵢ:

**Δaᵢ = |aᵢ − ā|**

Always take the **absolute value** — errors are never negative.

sections.heading: Mean Absolute Error
sections.body:
Average all individual absolute errors:

**Δā = (Δa₁ + Δa₂ + ... + Δaₙ) / n**

Final result reported as: **(ā ± Δā)**

This means the true value likely lies between ā − Δā and ā + Δā.

highlight: Mean absolute error = our uncertainty. The true value is within ā ± Δā with high confidence.

title: Absolute → Relative → Percentage Error

parts.meaning: Mean absolute error (same units as quantity)
Mean (best estimate) of the measured quantity

note: Relative error has no units. It tells you what fraction of the value is uncertain.
derived_from: Relative error = |uncertainty|/|value|. Multiply by 100 to express as percentage.

question: Five measurements of a length are: 2.62, 2.63, 2.61, 2.64, 2.60 cm. The mean absolute error is:
hint: Step 1: Find the mean. Step 2: Find |each value − mean|. Step 3: Average those.

sentence: If the mean value is 5.00 s and the mean absolute error is 0.05 s, the percentage error is _______.
explanation:
%Error = (Δā / ā) × 100 = (0.05 / 5.00) × 100 = **1%** ✓

Note: Relative error = 0.05/5.00 = 0.01 (dimensionless)

title: Error Propagation — The Core Rules

sections.heading: Why Propagation Matters
sections.body:
Derived quantities (density = mass/volume, speed = distance/time) depend on measured values. Errors in each measurement **combine** to give the error in the derived result.

JEE tests this regularly — learn these rules once, use them forever.

sections.heading: Rule 1: Addition & Subtraction
sections.body:
If Z = A + B  or  Z = A − B:

**ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB**

Absolute errors always ADD — regardless of + or − sign.

sections.heading: Rule 2: Multiplication & Division
sections.body:
If Z = A × B  or  Z = A / B:

**ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B**

Relative errors ADD for both multiplication and division.

sections.heading: Rule 3: Powers
sections.body:
If Z = Aᵖ Bq / Cʳ:

**ΔZ/Z = p(ΔA/A) + q(ΔB/B) + r(ΔC/C)**

The power **multiplies** the relative error of each quantity.

highlight: For Z = A³: ΔZ/Z = 3(ΔA/A). The exponent multiplies the error — this is the most-tested rule in JEE.

title: Error Propagation — Master Formula
formula: Z = AᵖBq/Cʳ  →  ΔZ/Z = p(ΔA/A) + q(ΔB/B) + r(ΔC/C)

parts.meaning: Absolute values of exponents/powers in the formula
Relative error in the derived quantity Z

note: Use ABSOLUTE values of powers even for division (denominator). Never use negative exponents.
derived_from: Take log: ln Z = p·ln A + q·ln B − r·ln C. Differentiate: dZ/Z = p·dA/A + q·dB/B + r·dC/C. For errors, use absolute values.

title: Error Propagation — Quick Reference
instruction: Tap each formula to see the error rule.

items.back:
ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB
Absolute errors add.

ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB
Absolute errors STILL add! (Common trap in JEE)

ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B
Relative errors add.

ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B
Relative errors add for division too.

ΔZ/Z = n × (ΔA/A)
Power multiplies the relative error.

ΔZ/Z = p(ΔA/A) + q(ΔB/B) + r(ΔC/C)
The master formula.

title: Worked Example: Error in Sum & Difference
problem: L₁ = (12.5 ± 0.2) cm and L₂ = (7.3 ± 0.1) cm. Find (a) L₁ + L₂ and (b) L₁ − L₂ with errors.

steps.detail:
L₁ = 12.5 cm,  ΔL₁ = 0.2 cm
L₂ = 7.3 cm,   ΔL₂ = 0.1 cm

Difference = 12.5 − 7.3 = 5.2 cm

Error: ΔZ = ΔL₁ + ΔL₂ = 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 cm

Result: **(5.2 ± 0.3) cm**

The error is IDENTICAL in both cases (0.3 cm).

Absolute errors always ADD — whether you add or subtract the quantities. This is the #1 trap in JEE for this topic!

title: Worked Example: Error in Powers — Sphere Volume
problem: Radius of a sphere: r = (2.10 ± 0.05) cm. Find the percentage error in its volume V = (4/3)πr³.

steps.detail:
V = (4/3)πr³

The constant (4/3)π has zero error. Only r contributes.
Power of r = **3**.

ΔV/V = 3 × (Δr/r)

The exponent 3 multiplies the relative error of r.

Percentage error in volume ≈ **7.1%**

💡 The volume error is TRIPLE the radius error because V ∝ r³.
This scaling by powers is the key JEE concept.

question: T = 2π√(L/g). If L has 2% error and g has 3% error, the % error in T is:
explanation:
T = 2π × L^(1/2) × g^(−1/2)

ΔT/T = (1/2)(ΔL/L) + (1/2)(Δg/g)

= (1/2)(2%) + (1/2)(3%) = 1% + 1.5% = **2.5%** ✓

Note: Use |power| = 1/2 for both L and g. Constants 2π have no error.
hint: Rewrite T as L^(1/2) × g^(-1/2). Power of each is 1/2. Apply: ΔT/T = (1/2)(ΔL/L) + (1/2)(Δg/g)

question: E = p²/(2m). If % error in momentum p is 1% and % error in mass m is 2%, the % error in E is:
explanation:
E = p² × (2m)⁻¹ → power of p is 2, power of m is 1

ΔE/E = 2(Δp/p) + 1(Δm/m)

= 2(1%) + 1(2%) = 2% + 2% = **4%** ✓

(The constant 2 in denominator has no error. |power of m| = 1)
hint: Write E = p² × m⁻¹. Power of p = 2, power of m = 1. Apply error formula.

title: ⚡ JEE Shortcut: Max % Error in Any Formula
body:
For Z = AᵃBᵇ/CᶜDᵈ:

**% error in Z = a(%ΔA) + b(%ΔB) + c(%ΔC) + d(%ΔD)**

All terms POSITIVE (absolute powers). The variable with the HIGHEST power contributes the MOST error.

💡 Strategy: if two measurements have equal % error, the one raised to a higher power dominates.

quick.label: B³ gives 3× more error contribution than C¹ for same % error

question: R = V/I where V = (100 ± 2) V and I = (10 ± 0.5) A. The % error in R is:
hint: For R = V/I: relative errors add. Calculate % error in V and I separately, then add.

instruction: Match the formula to the correct error propagation rule:
explanation:
√A = A^(1/2) so power = 1/2 → ΔZ/Z = (1/2)(ΔA/A).
For Z = A − B: same rule as addition — ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB (errors add regardless of sign).

title: Significant Figures — What and Why

sections.heading: What Are Significant Figures?
sections.body:
Significant figures (SF or sig figs) are the **meaningful digits** in a measurement.

They reflect the precision of the measuring instrument:
• 3.46 cm (3 SF) → read to nearest 0.01 cm
• 3.4 cm (2 SF) → read to nearest 0.1 cm

sections.heading: Why It Matters in JEE
sections.body:
JEE Numerical Value questions and result expression require correct sig figs.

• Over-reporting: 2.5 × 3.1 = 7.75 → should be **7.8** (2 SF)
• Under-reporting: 2.50 × 3.10 = 7.75 → correct to **3 SF** = 7.75

highlight: Sig figs = precision of measurement. Never report more precision than your instrument provides.

title: Significant Figure Counting Rules
caption: Apply these rules in order. Scientific notation removes all ambiguity.
html:
RuleExampleSF
Non-zero digits: always significant3.463
Zeros between non-zeros: significant3.0464
Leading zeros: NOT significant0.00342
Trailing zeros after decimal: significant3.4604
Trailing zeros in integer: ambiguous34002,3 or 4
Scientific notation: all mantissa digits3.40×10³3
💡 Tip: Use scientific notation to remove all ambiguity about trailing zeros!

title: Tap to Reveal: Sig Fig Rules with Examples
instruction: Tap each rule to reveal examples.

items.back:
All non-zero digits are significant.
3.46 → 3 SF | 28.9 → 3 SF | 1234 → 4 SF

Zeros trapped between non-zero digits are significant.
3.046 → 4 SF | 1001 → 4 SF | 40.05 → 4 SF

Zeros to the LEFT of all non-zero digits: NOT significant.
0.0034 → 2 SF | 0.04 → 1 SF | 0.007 → 1 SF

Trailing zeros to the RIGHT of the decimal point ARE significant.
3.460 → 4 SF | 5.00 → 3 SF | 12.0 → 3 SF

Ambiguous without a decimal point.
3400 → could be 2, 3, or 4 SF
Write 3.40 × 10³ to show 3 SF clearly.

question: How many significant figures are in the number 0.00340?
explanation:
Breaking down 0.00340:
• '0.00' — leading zeros → NOT significant
• '3' → significant (non-zero digit)
• '4' → significant (non-zero digit)
• '0' — trailing zero after decimal → significant

Total = **3 significant figures** ✓

In scientific notation: 3.40 × 10⁻³ (3 SF is clear)
hint: Leading zeros (before the 3) are not significant. The trailing zero after 4 IS significant because it follows the decimal.

title: Sig Figs in Arithmetic Operations

sections.heading: Addition & Subtraction
sections.body:
Round result to the **least number of decimal places** among all numbers.

Example:
12.4 + 3.52 + 0.123 = 16.043
→ 12.4 has fewest decimal places (1)
→ Answer: **16.0** (1 decimal place)

sections.heading: Multiplication & Division
sections.body:
Round result to the **least number of significant figures** among all numbers.

Example:
2.5 × 3.14 = 7.85
→ 2.5 has fewest SF (2)
→ Answer: **7.9** (2 SF)

sections.heading: Rounding Rules
sections.body:
• Digit to drop < 5 → leave preceding digit unchanged
• Digit to drop > 5 → increase preceding digit by 1
• Digit to drop = 5 → round to even (2.45 → 2.4, 2.35 → 2.4)

highlight: Addition/Subtraction → match DECIMAL PLACES. Multiplication/Division → match SIG FIGS. Two different rules!

sentence: The result of 2.33 × 4.1 reported to the correct number of significant figures is _______.
explanation:
2.33 × 4.1 = 9.553

Sig figs: 2.33 has 3 SF, 4.1 has **2 SF** → answer must have 2 SF.

9.553 rounded to 2 SF = **9.6** ✓

(The '5' in 9.553 rounds up the 9.5 to 9.6)

title: ⚡ Order of Magnitude — Quick Concept
body:
Order of magnitude = the power of 10 nearest to the number.

Method:
1. Write in scientific notation: N × 10ᵖ
2. If N < √10 ≈ 3.162 → order = 10ᵖ
3. If N ≥ 3.162 → order = 10ᵖ⁺¹

Examples:
• 4500 = 4.5 × 10³ → 4.5 > 3.162 → order = 10⁴
• 2000 = 2.0 × 10³ → 2.0 < 3.162 → order = 10³

question: The result of (14.5 + 1.234 − 3.24) expressed to correct significant figures is:
explanation:
14.5 + 1.234 − 3.24 = 12.494

For addition/subtraction → match DECIMAL PLACES:
• 14.5 → **1 decimal place** (least)
• 1.234 → 3 decimal places
• 3.24 → 2 decimal places

Round 12.494 to 1 decimal place = **12.5** ✓
hint: For addition/subtraction: find which number has the fewest decimal places. Round the answer to match.

explanation:
Breaking down 0.003050:
• '0.00' — leading zeros → NOT significant
• '3' → significant
• '0' — captive zero (between 3 and 5) → significant
• '5' → significant
• '0' — trailing zero after decimal → significant

Total = **4 significant figures** ✓

mistakes.mistake: Subtracting errors: writing ΔZ = ΔA − ΔB for Z = A − B
mistakes.fix: Absolute errors ALWAYS add. For Z = A − B, the error is ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB. Subtracting errors would dangerously underestimate the uncertainty.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring the power: writing ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A for Z = A³
mistakes.fix: For Z = A³: ΔZ/Z = 3(ΔA/A). The exponent (3) multiplies the relative error. If power = 2, multiply by 2. Always.

mistakes.mistake: Using the wrong type of error: mixing absolute error with relative error
mistakes.fix: Addition/subtraction uses absolute errors (ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB). Multiplication/division uses relative errors (ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B). Don't cross-use them.

mistakes.mistake: Counting leading zeros as significant: treating 0.0034 as having 4 SF
mistakes.fix: 0.0034 has only 2 SF. The '0.00' only positions the decimal — it carries no precision information.

mistakes.mistake: Using multiplication rules for addition: rounding 14.5 + 1.234 to 3 SF instead of 1 decimal place
mistakes.fix: Addition → round to fewest DECIMAL PLACES. Multiplication → round to fewest SF. These are completely different rules.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to report trailing zeros: writing 3.4 instead of 3.40 after calculation
mistakes.fix: 3.40 and 3.4 mean different things: 3.40 = 3 SF (measured to 0.01), 3.4 = 2 SF (measured to 0.1). Trailing zeros after the decimal matter.

title: Spot the Mistake: Error Propagation Statements
instruction: One of these statements is WRONG. Which one?

sentences.text: The mean absolute error is always a positive quantity.
For Z = A × B, the relative error is ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B.
For Z = A − B, the absolute error is ΔZ = ΔA − ΔB.
sentences.explanation: WRONG — For Z = A − B, the absolute error is ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB (always add). Subtracting errors would underestimate the true uncertainty, which is physically invalid.

sentences.text: For Z = Aⁿ, the relative error is ΔZ/Z = n × (ΔA/A).

instruction: Arrange these steps in order to find the % error in g = 4π²L/T²:
words: Write the error formula: Δg/g = ΔL/L + 2(ΔT/T)
correct: Write the error formula: Δg/g = ΔL/L + 2(ΔT/T)|Calculate % error in L: (ΔL/L)×100|Calculate % error in T: (ΔT/T)×100|Add: %Δg = %ΔL + 2×(%ΔT)
explanation:
Step 1: Always write the error propagation formula for the given expression first.
Step 2-3: Find % errors for each variable.
Step 4: Combine — T gets multiplied by 2 because its power in the formula is 2.

title: Worked Example: Full JEE-Style Problem — Finding g
problem: A simple pendulum has L = (1.00 ± 0.01) m and T = (2.00 ± 0.02) s. Using g = 4π²L/T², find g and its % error.

steps.detail:
g = (4π²) × L × T⁻²

Δg/g = ΔL/L + 2 × (ΔT/T)

(Constant 4π² has no error. Power of L is 1, power of T is 2.)

steps.step: Find % errors in L and T

steps.detail:
g = **(9.87 ± 0.30) m/s²**

💡 T contributes 2× more to error because its power in the formula is 2. Even though both L and T have 1% individual error, T doubles its contribution.

question: A Vernier caliper has 1 MSD = 1 mm. Its Vernier scale has 50 divisions such that 50 VSD = 49 MSD. The least count of this Vernier caliper is:
explanation:
LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD

50 VSD = 49 MSD → 1 VSD = 49/50 mm = 0.98 mm

LC = 1.00 − 0.98 = **0.02 mm** ✓

Alternatively: LC = MSD/n = 1/50 mm = 0.02 mm

This is finer than the standard 0.1 mm Vernier — 50-division Verniers are used for more precise measurements.
hint: LC = 1 MSD / n where n = total Vernier divisions = 50

question: The density of a material is calculated using ρ = M/V where volume V is measured using a cube of side L. If the % error in measuring M is 1.5% and in measuring L is 1%, the % error in density ρ is:
explanation:
ρ = M / V = M / L³

Δρ/ρ = ΔM/M + 3(ΔL/L)

%Error in ρ = %Error in M + 3 × %Error in L

= 1.5% + 3 × 1% = 1.5% + 3% = **4.5%** ✓

Key: V = L³ → power of L is 3, so 3 × 1% = 3% contribution from L.
hint: V = L³ so ΔV/V = 3(ΔL/L). Then ρ = M/V → Δρ/ρ = ΔM/M + ΔV/V.

question: Z = A³B²/(C·√D). The % errors in A, B, C, D are 1%, 2%, 3%, 4% respectively. The maximum % error in Z is:
hint: Powers: A has 3, B has 2, C has 1, D has 1/2 (since √D = D^0.5). Multiply each power by its % error and sum all.

question: A Vernier caliper (LC = 0.1 mm) has a positive zero error of 0.3 mm. The main scale reads 2.3 cm and the 4th Vernier division coincides with a main scale line. The corrected measurement is:
explanation:
Raw reading = MS reading + (Coinciding VSD × LC)
= 2.3 cm + (4 × 0.01 cm)
= 2.3 cm + 0.04 cm = 2.34 cm

Zero error = +0.3 mm = +0.03 cm (positive → subtract)

Corrected reading = 2.34 − 0.03 = **2.34 cm**

Wait: zero error = 0.3 mm = 0.03 cm
2.34 − 0.03 = 2.31 cm

Actually corrected = **2.31 cm**

Hmm — let me recalculate properly:
Raw = 23 mm + 4 × 0.1 mm = 23 + 0.4 = 23.4 mm
Zero error = +0.3 mm
Corrected = 23.4 − 0.3 = 23.1 mm = **2.31 cm** ✓
hint: Raw reading = MS + (VSD × LC). Then subtract positive zero error from raw reading.

instruction: Match the physical quantity to its % error formula:

meaning: LC(Vernier) = MSD/n | LC(Screw) = Pitch/N | Δā = Σ|aᵢ−ā|/n | %Error = (Δā/ā)×100 | Z=AᵖBq → ΔZ/Z = p(ΔA/A)+q(ΔB/B)
wrong: TRAP: For Z = A−B, error is ΔZ = ΔA+ΔB (NOT ΔA−ΔB). Errors always add, never subtract!
family: Add/Subtract → match decimal places for sig figs

title: 📝 Chapter Summary — What to Review Before JEE

sections.heading: Instruments & Least Count
sections.body:
• Metre scale: **1 mm**
• Vernier caliper: **1/n × MSD** (typically 0.1 mm or 0.05 mm)
• Screw gauge: **Pitch/N** (typically 0.01 mm)
• Always apply zero correction before reporting reading.

sections.heading: Error Analysis
sections.body:
• True value ≈ ā = arithmetic mean
• Absolute error: Δaᵢ = |aᵢ − ā|
• Mean absolute error: Δā = Σ|Δaᵢ|/n
• % error = (Δā/ā) × 100

sections.heading: Error Propagation (JEE Focus)
sections.body:
• **A ± B** → ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB
• **A × B or A/B** → ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B
• **Aⁿ** → ΔZ/Z = n(ΔA/A)
• **AᵖBq/Cʳ** → ΔZ/Z = p(ΔA/A)+q(ΔB/B)+r(ΔC/C)

sections.heading: Significant Figures
sections.body:
• Leading zeros: NOT significant
• Captive zeros: significant
• Trailing zeros after decimal: significant
• Add/Subtract → match **decimal places**
• Multiply/Divide → match **sig fig count**

highlight: JEE checklist: (1) Zero error correction (2) Correct error propagation formula (3) Correct sig figs in final answer. Get these right every time.
